https://aeon.co/essays/privacy-matters-b.standfirst: Philosopher Carissa Véliz argues that personal information creates leverage for whoever collects it, so privacy should be understood as a shared political and ethical concern rather than an individual preference for hiding things.
body: The question: Is privacy an individual consumer preference, or a shared political good?
The thesis: Véliz argues that collecting personal information concentrates power in those who can aggregate, analyze and trade it.
The argument starts from a familiar experience: data about ordinary routines can expose intimate details even without a direct confession.
The next step is collective: information about one person may also expose relatives, contacts and members of a group, so a personal decision to disclose has external effects.
A common objection is that a person with nothing to hide has little reason to care. The essay replies that power, manipulation and unequal bargaining positions matter even without secret wrongdoing.

A further tension is that information sharing can provide valuable services, research and convenience. The issue is how to constrain coercive accumulation and secondary use rather than ban information.
The practical implication is to assess privacy protections as public infrastructure, not merely personal hygiene.
The open question: Which information relationships can be made genuinely consensual when third parties are affected?
https://aeon.co/essays/privacy-matters-b.why_it_matters: The essay reframes routine data collection as a question about who can influence choices and how the costs spread beyond one person.
https://aeon.co/essays/privacy-matters-b.background: Digital services collect and combine information about people; an individual's disclosure can reveal information about others.
https://aeon.co/essays/privacy-matters-b.bigger_picture: Véliz treats privacy as a condition for autonomy and democratic power, not simply concealment of wrongdoing.
